idiom_name: int64_t minor units behind a currency-tagged value type (C++11)
implementation_notes: The default C++ realization is a fixed-scale integer: an std::int64_t count of minor units plus a currency tag wrapped in a small value type with constexpr-friendly operators, ==, < and a std::hash specialization, so it behaves like a number while refusing to mix units. That replaces the classic Money class hierarchy with two words and a handful of operators; the scale is data, and any operation that can produce a fraction (percentage, division, tax) must call an explicit round_to_currency() or an allocation helper instead of std::round on a double. Reach for an arbitrary-precision decimal only when the amount itself needs more scale than the currency's minor unit, for example accrual or per-unit pricing.
pitfalls: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so combining large balances needs __builtin_add_overflow or a wider intermediate before the addition.
Multiplying minor units by a double percentage reintroduces float error; keep the multiplier as integer basis points and round once, explicitly.
A hard-coded two-decimal scale silently breaks JPY and the three-decimal Gulf currencies, because nothing in the type knows the exponent.

variants.name: Boost.Multiprecision decimal with explicit rounding policies
variants.implementation_notes: When amounts carry more scale than the currency's minor unit (interest accrual, per-unit prices, exchange rates), represent the amount as a Boost.Multiprecision decimal - cpp_dec_float<N> is header-only, radix 10, and comes with a std::numeric_limits specialization - and keep rounding in policy objects, the approach libraries such as moneycpp take: rounding_policy_to_currency_digits(round_half_even()) applies the currency's digit count at the single place money is settled. The wrapper, the ISO 4217 table and the conversion policy are still hand-written, because the standard library has no money type.
pitfalls: cpp_dec_float operations truncate rather than round, so the rounding policy has to be applied explicitly at settlement.
A large Digits10 keeps the digits inside the object on the stack and can overflow it; cpp_dec_float_100 is not a harmless default.
Converting between cpp_dec_float precisions is a truncating, explicit narrowing conversion.
